title: Tech Stack Sorter: Frontend vs Backend vs DevOps
description: Do you know where React, Docker, PostgreSQL, and Redis belong? Sort 20 popular tech tools into the correct category -- Frontend, Backend, Database, or DevOps. Learn what each tool does and where it fits in a modern tech stack!
learning_objectives: Understand the four layers of a modern tech stack: Frontend, Backend, Database, DevOps
Learn what popular programming tools and frameworks are used for
Understand the difference between client-side and server-side technologies
Recognise database technologies and when to use relational vs NoSQL
Learn about DevOps tools for deployment, monitoring, and infrastructure

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read the name and description of each tech tool card
Drag the card to the correct category bucket: Frontend, Backend, Database, or DevOps
Get instant feedback -- green for correct, red for wrong placement
Double-click any card for detailed information about the technology
Sort all 20 tools correctly to achieve a perfect score!
tips: Frontend = what users see and interact with in a browser or app
Backend = server-side logic, APIs, and business rules
Database = where data is stored, queried, and managed
DevOps = tools for building, deploying, monitoring, and scaling applications

buckets.label: Frontend
buckets.description: Client-side technologies that run in the browser or device

buckets.label: Backend
buckets.description: Server-side technologies that handle logic and data processing

buckets.label: Database

buckets.label: DevOps

items.label: React
items.description: A JavaScript library by Meta for building user interfaces with reusable components.
items.details: React uses a virtual DOM for efficient updates. It powers Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp Web, and Netflix. Created in 2013, it's the most popular frontend framework globally.
items.fun_fact: React was first deployed on Facebook's News Feed in 2011, before it was open-sourced!

items.label: Node.js
items.description: A JavaScript runtime that lets you run JavaScript on the server side.
items.details: Node.js uses Chrome's V8 engine and is event-driven, making it great for real-time apps like chat servers. LinkedIn, PayPal, and Uber use Node.js.
items.fun_fact: Node.js was created by Ryan Dahl in 2009 because he was frustrated with Apache's limited connections!

items.label: PostgreSQL
items.description: A powerful open-source relational database known for reliability and SQL compliance.
items.details: PostgreSQL supports complex queries, JSON data, full-text search, and geographic data. It's used by Apple, Instagram, Spotify, and the Indian government's Aadhaar system.
items.fun_fact: PostgreSQL has been in development since 1986 -- older than Linux, Python, and JavaScript!

items.label: Docker
items.description: A platform that packages applications into containers for consistent deployment anywhere.
items.details: Docker containers are lightweight, portable, and ensure 'works on my machine' problems disappear. Every major tech company uses Docker for deployment.
items.fun_fact: Docker's whale logo is named 'Moby Dock' -- the containers on its back represent shipping containers!

items.label: Tailwind CSS
items.description: A utility-first CSS framework for rapidly building custom user interfaces.
items.details: Instead of pre-built components, Tailwind gives you utility classes like 'text-blue-500' and 'p-4'. It's become the fastest-growing CSS framework since 2020.
items.fun_fact: Tailwind's creator Adam Wathan built it because he was tired of naming CSS classes!

items.label: Flask (Python)
items.description: A lightweight Python web framework for building APIs and web applications.
items.details: Flask is a micro-framework -- it gives you the basics and lets you add what you need. Pinterest, LinkedIn, and Netflix use Flask for microservices.
items.fun_fact: Flask started as an April Fools' joke! Creator Armin Ronacher released it on April 1, 2010!

items.label: MongoDB
items.description: A NoSQL document database that stores data as flexible JSON-like documents.
items.details: Unlike tables in SQL databases, MongoDB stores data as documents (like JSON objects). Great for rapidly changing data and prototyping. Used by eBay, Adobe, and BYJU'S.
items.fun_fact: MongoDB comes from 'humongous' -- it was designed to handle humongous amounts of data!

items.label: Kubernetes (K8s)
items.description: An open-source system for automatically deploying and scaling containerised apps.
items.details: Kubernetes orchestrates Docker containers across multiple servers. It handles load balancing, auto-scaling, and self-healing. Google donated it to open-source in 2014.
items.fun_fact: K8s is short for Kubernetes -- the 8 represents the 8 letters between 'K' and 's'!

items.label: Vue.js
items.description: A progressive JavaScript framework for building interactive web interfaces.
items.details: Vue is known for being easy to learn while being powerful enough for complex apps. Alibaba, Xiaomi, and GitLab use Vue.js. Created by Evan You, a former Google engineer.
items.fun_fact: Vue.js was created by one person and now has more GitHub stars than React!

items.label: Django (Python)
items.description: A high-level Python web framework that follows the 'batteries included' philosophy.
items.details: Django includes an admin panel, ORM, authentication, and more out of the box. Instagram, Mozilla, Disqus, and National Geographic use Django.
items.fun_fact: Django is named after jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt, who played with only two fingers on his left hand!

items.label: Redis
items.description: An in-memory data store used as a cache, message broker, and real-time database.
items.details: Redis stores data in RAM for lightning-fast reads and writes. It's used for caching, session management, leaderboards, and real-time analytics. Twitter, GitHub, and Snapchat rely on Redis.
items.fun_fact: Redis stands for 'REmote DIctionary Server' and can handle millions of operations per second!

items.label: GitHub Actions
items.description: A CI/CD platform built into GitHub for automating build, test, and deploy workflows.
items.details: GitHub Actions runs automated pipelines when you push code. It can run tests, build Docker images, deploy to AWS, and send notifications -- all triggered by git events.
items.fun_fact: GitHub Actions was launched in 2019 and is now used by over 50% of all GitHub repositories!

items.label: TypeScript
items.description: A typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript for better code quality.
items.details: TypeScript adds type checking to JavaScript, catching errors before runtime. Created by Microsoft, it's used in Angular, VS Code, and most modern frontend projects.
items.fun_fact: TypeScript was created by Anders Hejlsberg, who also created C# and Turbo Pascal!

items.label: Express.js
items.description: A minimal Node.js framework for building web APIs and server-side applications.
items.details: Express is the most popular Node.js backend framework, handling routing, middleware, and HTTP requests. It's the 'E' in the MERN/MEAN stack.
items.fun_fact: Express was inspired by Ruby's Sinatra framework and was first released in 2010!

items.label: Firebase
items.description: Google's platform with real-time database, authentication, and hosting for web and mobile apps.
items.details: Firebase provides a real-time NoSQL database, user authentication, cloud functions, and hosting in one package. Many Indian startups use Firebase for rapid prototyping.
items.fun_fact: Firebase was originally a chat app called Envolve before pivoting to become a backend platform!

items.label: NGINX
items.description: A high-performance web server and reverse proxy used to serve websites and load-balance traffic.
items.details: NGINX handles millions of concurrent connections efficiently. It serves as a reverse proxy, load balancer, and HTTP cache. Powers over 30% of all websites globally.
items.fun_fact: NGINX was created by Igor Sysoev in 2004 to solve the C10K problem -- handling 10,000 simultaneous connections!

items.label: Flutter
items.description: Google's UI toolkit for building natively compiled mobile, web, and desktop apps from one codebase.
items.details: Flutter uses Dart language and renders its own widgets for pixel-perfect UI on iOS and Android. Google Pay, Alibaba, and many Indian apps like Paytm use Flutter.
items.fun_fact: Flutter's hot reload feature lets developers see code changes in under 1 second!

items.label: GraphQL
items.description: A query language for APIs that lets clients request exactly the data they need.
items.details: Unlike REST where each endpoint returns fixed data, GraphQL lets the frontend ask for specific fields. Created by Facebook in 2012, used by GitHub, Shopify, and Swiggy.
items.fun_fact: GraphQL was created to solve Facebook's mobile app performance issues -- the News Feed was too slow with REST!

items.label: Elasticsearch
items.description: A distributed search and analytics engine for log data, full-text search, and real-time queries.
items.details: Elasticsearch powers search functionality on Wikipedia, GitHub, Netflix, and Uber. It can search through billions of documents in milliseconds.
items.fun_fact: Elasticsearch was created because its founder's wife needed a recipe search engine!

items.label: Terraform
items.description: An infrastructure-as-code tool that lets you define cloud resources using configuration files.
items.details: Terraform creates servers, databases, and networks on AWS, Azure, or GCP using code instead of clicking buttons. This makes infrastructure reproducible and version-controlled.
items.fun_fact: Terraform's creator HashiCorp was started by two college friends in a dorm room!

glossary_terms.definition: The mental effort required to process information and make decisions.
glossary_terms.example: Having too many options at once makes decisions harder and slower.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Working memory has limits. Experts chunk information into patterns, reducing cognitive load and enabling faster decisions.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Experienced doctors diagnose faster not because they think harder, but because they recognize patterns instantly.

glossary_terms.definition: Identifying recurring structures or relationships in information.
glossary_terms.example: Noticing that certain question types always have two plausible answers helps you focus faster.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Pattern recognition is a core skill in chess, medicine, engineering, and sport. It develops through deliberate practice.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Air traffic controllers recognize dangerous flight patterns faster than computers because of years of pattern training.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to direct mental attention toward what matters most and ignore distractions.
glossary_terms.example: Under time pressure, completing questions you're confident about before tackling harder ones.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Focus is a trainable skill. The Pomodoro method, mindfulness, and deliberate practice all improve sustained attention.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Olympic athletes train mental focus as rigorously as physical skills — pressure performance depends on it.

coaching_moment: Notice how each decision here requires weighing multiple options. Strategic thinkers pause before choosing — what's the long-term implication of each answer?
cultural_context: India produces more software engineers than any other country, yet employability in technology remains a challenge due to skills gaps. Tech Stack Sorter: Frontend vs Backend vs DevOps builds the logical and computational thinking that is foundational for India's tech workforce.
